steps.caption: Your eyes have four guards. The eyebrows stop sweat, the eyelids close to clean and protect the eye, the eyelashes catch dust, and tears wash the eye and keep it wet.

parts.label: eyebrow
parts.info: A curved line of hair above the eye that stops sweat from running into it.

parts.label: eyelid
parts.info: A fold of skin that closes to clean and protect the eye.

parts.label: eyelashes
parts.info: Short hairs on the edge of the eyelids that catch dust like a tiny brush.

parts.label: tears
parts.info: A salty liquid that washes the eye and keeps it wet.

steps.caption: Memory trick: the eyelid is the lid of the eye, like the lid on a pot. The eyelashes are a tiny brush that sweeps dust away, and the eyebrow is an umbrella that keeps sweat out.
At the front of the eye, light passes through the cornea, a clear window. The iris is the coloured ring, and the pupil is the black opening in its centre.

parts.label: cornea
parts.info: The clear window at the front of the eye that lets light in.

parts.label: iris
parts.info: The coloured ring that makes the pupil bigger or smaller.

parts.label: pupil
parts.info: The black opening in the centre of the iris where light enters the eye.

steps.caption: The iris controls how much light gets in. In bright light it makes the pupil smaller; in the dark it makes the pupil bigger so that more light can enter.

parts.label: iris
parts.info: The coloured ring that controls how much light gets in.

parts.label: pupil
parts.info: The opening that gets smaller in bright light and bigger in the dark.

steps.caption: Memory trick: Iris was the Greek goddess of the rainbow, so iris = coloured ring. The pupil is the dark doorway in the middle of the rainbow.
Behind the pupil, the lens focuses the light onto the retina, at the back of the eye. The retina is covered with light-sensitive cells. The optic nerve carries the message to the brain.

parts.label: lens
parts.info: A clear, flexible disc that focuses light onto the retina.

parts.label: retina
parts.info: The back of the eye, covered with cells that sense light.

parts.label: optic nerve
parts.info: Carries the message from the retina to the brain.

steps.caption: Memory trick: the retina is a cinema screen where the film arrives upside down. The brain is the projectionist who turns the picture the right way up.

tiles.label: brain: turns it the right way up

steps.caption: Follow the story of light: it enters through the cornea, passes the pupil, is focused by the lens and lands on the retina. Then the optic nerve tells the brain.
Test yourself: read each clue, say the word, then tap the card to check.

questions.prompt: Which part of the eye is the black opening in the centre?
questions.explanation: The pupil is the black opening in the centre of the eye; the iris is the coloured ring around it.

questions.prompt: Which part of the eye is the coloured ring that controls how much light gets in?
questions.explanation: The iris is the coloured ring; it makes the pupil smaller or bigger to control the light.

questions.prompt: Which tiny hairs catch dust before it gets into your eye?
questions.explanation: The eyelashes catch dust like a tiny brush; the eyebrows stop sweat.

questions.prompt: Which clear window at the front of the eye does light pass through first?
questions.explanation: The cornea is the clear window at the front of the eye; light passes through it before the pupil and the lens.

questions.prompt: How many eyelids does each eye have?
questions.explanation: Each eye has 2 eyelids, an upper eyelid and a lower eyelid, which close to clean and protect the eye.

questions.prompt: Which nerve carries the message from the eye to the brain?
questions.explanation: The optic nerve carries the message from the retina to the brain.

questions.prompt: What happens to your pupil in bright light?
questions.explanation: In bright light the iris makes the pupil smaller to let less light in; in the dark the pupil gets bigger.

questions.prompt: Which part of the eye focuses light onto the retina?
questions.explanation: The lens focuses light onto the retina, like a magnifying glass.

questions.prompt: On which part of the eye does the image arrive upside down?
questions.explanation: The image arrives upside down on the retina, at the back of the eye; the brain turns it the right way up.

questions.prompt: Which salty liquid washes your eyes and keeps them wet?
questions.explanation: Tears wash the eye and keep it wet.

questions.prompt: Which hairs above your eyes stop sweat running into them?
questions.explanation: The eyebrows stop sweat running into your eyes, like an umbrella.

questions.prompt: Light, cornea, pupil, lens, retina, optic nerve, brain. In which position is the lens?
questions.explanation: Light passes the cornea (2) and the pupil (3); then the lens (4) focuses it onto the retina.

steps.caption: Every sound is a vibration. Sound waves travel through the air from the thing that vibrates to your ears.
The outer ear has two parts. The pinna, the ear flap you can see, collects sound waves like a funnel, and the ear canal carries them inside. Earwax in the ear canal traps dust and germs.

parts.label: pinna
parts.info: The ear flap you can see, which collects sound waves like a funnel.

parts.label: ear canal
parts.info: The tunnel that carries sound waves from the pinna to the eardrum.

parts.label: earwax
parts.info: A sticky wax in the ear canal that traps dust and germs.

steps.caption: In the middle ear, sound waves hit the eardrum and make it vibrate. The vibration passes along three tiny bones called the ossicles: the hammer, the anvil and the stirrup.

parts.label: eardrum
parts.info: A thin skin that vibrates like a drum when sound waves hit it.

parts.label: hammer
parts.info: The first ossicle, joined to the eardrum, which passes the vibration on.

parts.label: anvil
parts.info: The middle ossicle, which passes the vibration from the hammer to the stirrup.

parts.label: stirrup
parts.info: The last ossicle and the smallest bone in the body, which passes the vibration to the inner ear.

steps.caption: Memory trick: ear + drum. The eardrum is a thin skin stretched like a drum; sound waves beat it and it vibrates.
Memory trick: Hammer, Anvil, Stirrup = H-A-S. Your middle ear HAS three tiny bones. The stirrup is the smallest bone in the human body.

In the inner ear, the cochlea is full of liquid and tiny hair cells that turn vibrations into nerve messages. The semicircular canals help you keep your balance, and the auditory nerve carries the message to the brain.

parts.label: cochlea
parts.info: A snail-shaped tube full of liquid and hair cells that turn vibrations into nerve messages.

parts.label: semicircular canals
parts.info: Three half circles full of liquid that help you keep your balance.

parts.label: auditory nerve
parts.info: Carries the message from the cochlea to the brain.

steps.caption: Memory trick: cochlea comes from the Latin word for a snail shell, so picture a tiny snail curled up in your ear. The semicircular canals are three half circles, like a roller coaster that tells you which way is up.

Follow the story of a sound: sound waves enter the pinna, travel down the ear canal, beat the eardrum and shake the ossicles. The liquid in the cochlea ripples, and the auditory nerve tells the brain.
Test yourself: read each clue, say the word, then tap the card to check.

questions.prompt: What is the ear flap you can see on the side of your head called?
questions.explanation: The pinna is the ear flap you can see; it collects sound waves like a funnel.

questions.prompt: What travels through the air and carries sound to your ears?
questions.explanation: Sound waves are vibrations that travel through the air to your ears.

questions.prompt: How many ossicles (tiny bones) are there in the middle ear?
questions.explanation: There are 3 ossicles: the hammer, the anvil and the stirrup. Remember H-A-S: your middle ear HAS three bones.

questions.prompt: Which thin skin vibrates when sound waves hit it?
questions.explanation: The eardrum is a thin skin stretched like a drum; sound waves make it vibrate.

questions.prompt: What traps dust and germs in the ear canal?
questions.explanation: Earwax in the ear canal traps dust and germs and protects the ear.

questions.prompt: Which part of the inner ear is shaped like a snail shell?
questions.explanation: The cochlea is shaped like a snail shell and is full of liquid and hair cells.

questions.prompt: Which ossicle is the smallest bone in the human body?
questions.explanation: The stirrup is the smallest bone in the human body; it is the last of the three ossicles.

questions.prompt: Which parts of the inner ear help you keep your balance?
questions.explanation: The semicircular canals help you keep your balance; the cochlea is for hearing.

questions.prompt: Which nerve carries messages from the cochlea to the brain?
questions.explanation: The auditory nerve carries hearing messages from the cochlea to the brain.

questions.prompt: Remember the eye: which part focuses light onto the retina?
questions.explanation: The lens focuses light onto the retina at the back of the eye.

questions.prompt: Which ossicle sits between the hammer and the stirrup?
questions.explanation: The anvil sits between the hammer and the stirrup: Hammer, Anvil, Stirrup = H-A-S.

questions.prompt: Which tunnel carries sound waves from the pinna to the eardrum?
questions.explanation: The ear canal is the tunnel that carries sound waves from the pinna to the eardrum.

steps.caption: Things that smell give off tiny particles called odour molecules. They travel through the air, and when you breathe in, they enter your nose.

tiles.label: a flower gives off a smell

steps.caption: Air goes in through the two nostrils into the nasal cavity, the large space inside your nose.

parts.label: nostrils
parts.info: The two openings of the nose where air goes in.

parts.label: nasal cavity
parts.info: The large space inside the nose that air passes through.

steps.caption: The nasal cavity is lined with mucus, a sticky liquid. Mucus traps dust and germs, and it dissolves odour molecules so that they can be detected.

parts.label: mucus
parts.info: A sticky liquid lining the nasal cavity that traps dust and germs and dissolves odour molecules.

steps.caption: At the top of the nasal cavity are the olfactory receptors, special smell cells. They send a message along the olfactory nerve to the brain.

parts.label: olfactory receptors
parts.info: Smell cells at the top of the nasal cavity that detect odour molecules.

parts.label: olfactory nerve
parts.info: Carries the message from the olfactory receptors to the brain.

parts.label: brain
parts.info: Receives the message and tells you what you are smelling.

steps.caption: Memory trick: olfactory sounds like "oh, factory!" Picture a busy smell factory at the top of your nose, where the olfactory receptors work.
Memory trick: each odour molecule is a key and each olfactory receptor is a lock. When the key fits the lock, the receptor sends a message.
Smell and taste work together. When you have a cold and your nose is blocked, food seems to taste of less, because you cannot smell it.
Follow the story of a smell: odour molecules enter the nostrils and reach the nasal cavity. The olfactory receptors detect them, and the olfactory nerve tells the brain.
Test yourself: read each clue, say the word, then tap the card to check.

questions.prompt: What are the tiny particles that carry a smell through the air?
questions.explanation: Odour molecules are tiny particles that travel through the air and carry a smell to your nose.

questions.prompt: What are the two openings of your nose called?
questions.explanation: The nostrils are the two openings of the nose; air goes in through them.

questions.prompt: How many nostrils do you have?
questions.explanation: You have 2 nostrils, the two openings through which air enters the nose.

questions.prompt: Which sticky liquid in the nose traps dust and dissolves odour molecules?
questions.explanation: Mucus is the sticky liquid in the nose; it traps dust and dissolves odour molecules.

questions.prompt: What are the smell cells at the top of the nasal cavity called?
questions.explanation: The olfactory receptors are the smell cells at the top of the nasal cavity.

questions.prompt: What is the large space inside your nose called?
questions.explanation: The nasal cavity is the large space inside your nose, lined with mucus.

questions.prompt: Which nerve carries smell messages to the brain?
questions.explanation: The olfactory nerve carries smell messages from the olfactory receptors to the brain.

questions.prompt: Which sense works together with smell, so that food tastes of less when your nose is blocked?
questions.explanation: Smell and taste work together: with a blocked nose you cannot smell your food, so it seems to taste of less.

questions.prompt: Remember the ear: which ossicle is the smallest bone in the human body?
questions.explanation: The stirrup is the smallest bone in the human body.

questions.prompt: After the nostrils, where do odour molecules go next?
questions.explanation: After the nostrils, odour molecules reach the nasal cavity, where the olfactory receptors detect them.

questions.prompt: What does the word olfactory mean?
questions.explanation: Olfactory means to do with smell: olfactory receptors are smell cells and the olfactory nerve carries smell messages.

questions.prompt: Odour molecules, nostrils, nasal cavity, olfactory receptors, olfactory nerve, brain. In which position are the olfactory receptors?
questions.explanation: The olfactory receptors are in position 4: after the odour molecules (1), the nostrils (2) and the nasal cavity (3).

steps.caption: Your tongue is a strong muscle. When you eat, saliva in your mouth dissolves the food so that you can taste it.

parts.label: tongue
parts.info: A strong muscle that moves food around your mouth and helps you taste it.

steps.caption: The tongue is covered with small bumps called papillae. Inside the papillae are the taste buds, which contain taste receptor cells.

parts.label: papillae
parts.info: Small bumps that cover the tongue, like little hills.

parts.label: taste buds
parts.info: Groups of cells hidden inside the papillae, like flower buds.

parts.label: taste receptor cells
parts.info: Cells inside each taste bud that detect the taste of dissolved food.

steps.caption: Memory trick: the papillae are little hills on your tongue, and the taste buds are flower buds hiding in the hills.
There are five basic tastes: sweet, salty, sour, bitter and umami. Umami is the savoury taste of foods like cheese, tomatoes, mushrooms and meat broth.
Memory trick: "Sweet Sally Sees Big Umbrellas" = Sweet, Salty, Sour, Bitter, Umami. Count them on one hand: five tastes, five fingers.
Every area of the tongue can detect all five tastes. The old "tongue map", with one taste for each area, is a myth.
The taste receptor cells send messages along the taste nerves to the brain, which tells you what you are eating.

parts.label: taste receptor cells
parts.info: Cells in the taste buds that detect a taste and start the message.

parts.label: taste nerves
parts.info: Carry the message from the taste receptor cells to the brain.

steps.caption: Follow the story of a taste: saliva dissolves the food, which reaches the papillae and the taste buds inside them. The taste nerves tell the brain.
Test yourself: read each clue, say the word, then tap the card to check.

cards.front: A strong muscle in your mouth
A liquid that dissolves food so that you can taste it
The small bumps on the tongue
Groups of taste cells inside the papillae
The savoury taste of cheese and mushrooms
The taste of a lemon

questions.prompt: What are the small bumps on your tongue called?
questions.explanation: The papillae are the small bumps on the tongue; the taste buds are inside them.

questions.prompt: How many basic tastes are there?
questions.explanation: There are 5 basic tastes: sweet, salty, sour, bitter and umami.

questions.prompt: Which liquid in your mouth dissolves food so that you can taste it?
questions.explanation: Saliva dissolves food so that the taste buds can detect it.

questions.prompt: Which taste does a lemon have?
questions.explanation: A lemon tastes sour.

questions.prompt: What is found inside the papillae, with taste receptor cells?
questions.explanation: The taste buds are inside the papillae and contain the taste receptor cells.

questions.prompt: The tongue is a strong...
questions.explanation: The tongue is a strong muscle that moves food around your mouth.

questions.prompt: Which taste is the savoury taste of cheese, tomatoes and mushrooms?
questions.explanation: Umami is the savoury taste of cheese, tomatoes, mushrooms and meat broth.

questions.prompt: Which taste do coffee and dark chocolate have?
questions.explanation: Coffee and dark chocolate taste bitter.

questions.prompt: Which area of the tongue can detect salty tastes?
questions.explanation: Every area of the tongue detects all five tastes, salty too; the tongue map is a myth.

questions.prompt: Remember the nose: what are the smell cells at the top of the nasal cavity called?
questions.explanation: The olfactory receptors are the smell cells at the top of the nasal cavity.

questions.prompt: Which nerves carry taste messages to the brain?
questions.explanation: The taste nerves carry messages from the taste buds to the brain.

questions.prompt: Which taste do sweets and honey have?
questions.explanation: Sweets and honey taste sweet.

steps.caption: Your skin is the sense organ of touch. It covers your whole body, so it is the largest organ of the body.
Skin has three layers: the epidermis on the outside, the dermis in the middle and the hypodermis, a layer of fat, on the inside.

parts.label: epidermis
parts.info: The outer layer of the skin, which protects your body.

parts.label: dermis
parts.info: The middle layer of the skin, with most of the touch receptors.

parts.label: hypodermis
parts.info: The inner layer of the skin, made of fat that keeps you warm.

steps.caption: The dermis has most of the touch receptors, as well as the sweat glands and the roots of your hairs.

parts.label: touch receptors
parts.info: Tiny sensors in the dermis that feel what touches your skin.

parts.label: sweat gland
parts.info: A coiled tube that makes sweat to cool you down.

parts.label: hair root
parts.info: The bottom of a hair, deep in the skin, where the hair grows.

steps.caption: Memory trick: derma means skin. Epi means on top, so the epidermis is on top; hypo means under, so the hypodermis is underneath; the dermis is the skin in the middle.
Touch receptors detect pressure, temperature (heat and cold) and pain. Pain receptors warn you of danger.

parts.label: touch receptors
parts.info: Sensors that detect pressure, heat, cold and pain.

parts.label: nerve
parts.info: Carries the message from the touch receptors to the spinal cord and the brain.

steps.caption: Your fingertips and your lips have the most touch receptors, so they are the most sensitive parts of your skin.
Memory trick: read with your fingers, feel with your lips. People who are blind read Braille with their fingertips, because fingertips have so many receptors.
Follow the story of a touch: a stimulus presses the skin, the touch receptors in the dermis send a message along the nerves to the spinal cord and up to the brain.
Test yourself: read each clue, say the word, then tap the card to check.

The outer layer of the skin

questions.prompt: Which is the largest organ of the body?
questions.explanation: The skin is the largest organ of the body; it covers the whole body.

questions.prompt: How many layers does the skin have?
questions.explanation: The skin has 3 layers: the epidermis, the dermis and the hypodermis.

questions.prompt: What is the outer layer of the skin called?
questions.explanation: The epidermis is the outer layer of the skin: epi means on top.

questions.prompt: Which layer of the skin has most of the touch receptors?
questions.explanation: The dermis, the middle layer, has most of the touch receptors.

questions.prompt: What is the inner fat layer of the skin called?
questions.explanation: The hypodermis is the inner layer of fat: hypo means under.

questions.prompt: Which touch receptors warn you of danger?
questions.explanation: Pain receptors warn you of danger, so you can move away from it.

questions.prompt: Which parts of the body have the most touch receptors?
questions.explanation: The fingertips and the lips have the most touch receptors, so they are the most sensitive.

questions.prompt: A hot pan touches your hand. Which receptors detect the heat?
questions.explanation: Temperature receptors in the skin detect heat and cold.

questions.prompt: You press a button. Which touch receptors detect it?
questions.explanation: Pressure receptors in the skin detect pushing and pressing.

questions.prompt: Remember the tongue: which taste is the savoury taste of cheese and mushrooms?
questions.explanation: Umami is the savoury taste of cheese and mushrooms.

questions.prompt: In which layer of the skin are the sweat glands and the hair roots?
questions.explanation: The sweat glands and the hair roots are in the dermis, the middle layer of the skin.

questions.prompt: In the touch story, where does the message go just before the brain?
questions.explanation: The nerves carry the message from the touch receptors to the spinal cord and then up to the brain.

steps.caption: The central nervous system (CNS) is made of the brain and the spinal cord. The skull protects the brain, and the spine, or vertebral column, protects the spinal cord.

parts.label: brain
parts.info: The control centre of the body and part of the central nervous system (CNS).

parts.label: skull
parts.info: A hard case of bone that protects the brain.

parts.label: spinal cord
parts.info: A thick bundle of nerve fibres inside the spine, the other part of the CNS.

parts.label: spine
parts.info: The vertebral column, a chain of small bones that protects the spinal cord.

steps.caption: The peripheral nervous system (PNS) is all the nerves that connect the central nervous system with the rest of the body.

parts.label: nerves
parts.info: They form the peripheral nervous system (PNS), linking the CNS with every part of the body.

steps.caption: Nerves are made of neurons, or nerve cells. Each neuron has a cell body with a nucleus inside, the control centre of the cell.

parts.label: cell body
parts.info: The main part of the neuron, which keeps the cell alive.

parts.label: nucleus
parts.info: The control centre of the cell, inside the cell body.

steps.caption: Dendrites are short branches that receive messages. The axon is a long fibre that carries the message away from the cell body to the axon terminals.

parts.label: dendrites
parts.info: Short branches that receive messages, like doors in.

parts.label: axon
parts.info: A long fibre that carries the message away from the cell body.

parts.label: axon terminals
parts.info: The ends of the axon, which pass the message on to the next neuron.

steps.caption: Memory trick: the Axon sends the message Away; the Dendrites are the Doors where it comes in, and they branch like a tree.
A synapse is a tiny gap where a message passes from one neuron to the next. A nerve is a bundle of neuron fibres, like a cable full of wires.

parts.label: synapse
parts.info: A tiny gap where the message jumps from one neuron to the next.

steps.caption: Follow a message inside a neuron: it comes in through the dendrites, passes the cell body, runs along the axon to the axon terminals and jumps across the synapse to the next neuron.

Memory trick: Sensory nerves bring what you Sense into the CNS; Motor nerves make you Move by carrying orders from the CNS to the muscles. Receptors in the sense organs are where it all starts: they detect the stimuli.
A reflex act is very fast. If you touch something hot, the spinal cord orders the muscle to pull your hand away before the brain even notices.
Test yourself: read each clue, say the word, then tap the card to check.

questions.prompt: A neuron is a nerve cell. Where does the message leave the neuron to cross the synapse?
questions.explanation: The message leaves the neuron at the axon terminals and crosses the synapse to the next neuron.

questions.prompt: Which branches of a neuron receive messages?
questions.explanation: The dendrites are the doors where messages come in; they branch like a tree.

questions.prompt: Which long fibre carries the message away from the cell body?
questions.explanation: The axon carries the message away from the cell body: Axon = Away.

questions.prompt: What is the tiny gap where a message passes from one neuron to the next?
questions.explanation: A synapse is the tiny gap where a message passes from one neuron to the next.

questions.prompt: Stimulus, receptor, sensory nerve, spinal cord, motor nerve, muscle. In which position is the motor nerve?
questions.explanation: The motor nerve is in position 5: it carries the order from the spinal cord to the muscle.

questions.prompt: Which part of the neuron contains the nucleus?
questions.explanation: The nucleus is inside the cell body, the control centre of the neuron.

questions.prompt: What do we call a bundle of neuron fibres?
questions.explanation: A nerve is a bundle of neuron fibres, like a cable full of wires.

questions.prompt: The central nervous system is the brain and the spinal cord. Which bones protect the spinal cord?
questions.explanation: The spine, or vertebral column, protects the spinal cord; the skull protects the brain.

questions.prompt: Which system is made of all the nerves that connect the CNS with the rest of the body?
questions.explanation: The peripheral nervous system is all the nerves that connect the central nervous system with the rest of the body.

questions.prompt: Which nerves carry messages from the receptors in the sense organs to the CNS?
questions.explanation: Sensory nerves carry what you sense from the receptors to the CNS; motor nerves carry orders to the muscles.

questions.prompt: You touch a hot pan and pull your hand away before you notice. Which organ controls this reflex act?
questions.explanation: A reflex act is controlled by the spinal cord, before the brain notices.

questions.prompt: Remember the skin: which layer of the skin is on the outside?
questions.explanation: The epidermis is the outer layer of the skin: epi means on top.
